A tool written in GoScheme, and the one test its writing was missing.

### `scripts/scmc-disassemble.scm`

Reads a `.scmc` bytecode file and prints what is in it: the chunks that are
still source as themselves, and every compiled body as its instructions with the
literals they mention.

```sh
goscheme compile hello.scm
goscheme scripts/scmc-disassemble.scm hello.scmc            # to the terminal
goscheme scripts/scmc-disassemble.scm hello.scmc -o out.scm
goscheme scripts/scmc-disassemble.scm --check hello.scmc    # a one-line summary
```

It is also the largest program in this repository written **in GoScheme rather
than Go**, which is most of the point.  It reads a binary file a byte at a time,
decodes Go's varints and zig-zag integers by hand, parses a tagged recursive
format whose values can hold compiled code inside compiled code, walks that
tree, and prints it.  Beyond R7RS it needs `(goscheme fast)` for `bit-and` and
`bit-shift`, and binary ports for the file; everything else is `(scheme base)`,
`(scheme write)`, `(scheme file)` and `(scheme process-context)`.  No part of it
is Go.

The output is a disassembly, not the original source: the compiler does not keep
the source, and a compiled body has no expressions left, only instructions.  The
chunks that are still source — an `import`, a top-level `define-syntax`, an
`include` — are printed verbatim, because that is how the file stores them.

`make check-disasm` runs it over the R7RS suite and the extension suite and
asserts that everything it printed reads back as Scheme: 22058 forms for the
reference suite, 5185 for the extensions.

### A regression test for shadowed bindings

Writing that script turned up a name-shadowing case worth pinning down: a
binding whose initializer mentions the same name refers to the binding *outside*
the one being made, an internal `define` shadows an outer binding of the same
name for the whole body, and a definition that reads another definition before
it has run is an error rather than a stale value.  The compiler got one of those
wrong until 3.1.0 (the internal-definition case, fixed in `5d3c52b`); all three
now have a test in the differential corpus, which is 65 programs run three ways.
